Colorado State Representative Richardson (R HD-56) shares his perspectives on the background of the ACA and the government shutdown.. 👇

“The Hidden Cost of “Temporary” Tax Credits
Why ACA Subsidies Are Part of the Shut Down Fight

Fifteen years ago in the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, the ACA, or Obama Care as it is commonly called, was passed.  One would think that health care would be more affordable by now.  But, as retiring Congresswoman Pelosi pointed out – it had to be passed to know what was in it.  Apparently, a lot.  And most of it is tremendously expensive. 

It has now come the heart of argument regarding the government shut down.  A shut that is now leaving our most vulnerable without SNAP benefits, our air traffic control system stressed, and our military unpaid.  So, how did we get to where we are today?  

In 2021, Congress expanded the Affordable Care Act’s premium tax credits. Those subsidies lower the cost of plans for individuals who buy health insurance through the federal and state exchanges. It sounded like good news for families struggling with rising insurance costs. But few realized that these larger subsidies were never meant to last, and that their expiration in 2025 was baked into the law from day one.

Here’s how we got here. The original ACA (Obama Care) tax credits were permanent, providing help on a sliding scale up to 400% of the federal poverty level (FPL). Above that threshold, families were on their own. The American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA)—passed in 2021 by a Democratic Congress and signed by President Biden—temporarily boosted those credits. It reduced the amount families had to pay for coverage and, for the first time, eliminated the 400% FPL cap entirely. Even higher-income households could qualify if their premiums consumed a big share of income. But that expansion was authorized only for two years.  Two years in which health insurance costs continued to grow.

In 2022, Democrats extended those temporary provisions for three more years through the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). Once again, the law set a firm expiration—this time at the end of 2025. Three more years in which the unlaying cost of health insurance rose.  That sunset wasn’t a drafting error; it was a deliberate budget tactic. Making the expansion permanent would have added more than $338 billion to the ten-year federal deficit score. By calling the program “temporary,” the drafters could fit it within the Senate’s “reconciliation” rules and claim a smaller fiscal impact. In Washington-speak, that’s called scoring, but to most Americans, it looks like an accounting trick.

Of course, once voters become accustomed to a benefit, it’s politically difficult to let it end. That’s the hidden strategy—create a costly new entitlement, call it temporary, and later pressure Congress to extend it again in the name of “fairness.” The real debate ahead isn’t whether the tax credits expire—it’s whether taxpayers can afford another round of temporary promises that somehow never seem to go away.

Facts and truth are important when public policy decisions must be made.  Unfortunately, both are too often masked in order to put a positive spin on legislation.  The Affordable Care Act has not produced affordable care.  It has masked the true and ever rising costs of health insurance – and in many ways has driven it.”
